comment: Tax presets keyed by store location. Shipped, read-only, editable without a rebuild — a rate change is a one-line edit here, not a code release. 'standardRatePercent' seeds every payment method when a shop picks this location, and in a tax-inclusive location it is the ONLY rate in play: the per-method matrix is not consulted there, because a value-added tax cannot vary by how a sale is settled. The tax-EXCLUSIVE entries (Canada, the US) deliberately quote NO standard rate: sales tax is added separately at settlement there, so 0 seeds every payment method tax free and the shop enters the rate it is registered to collect in Shop Settings — a shipped provincial or state rate is only ever a guess at what one particular store charges. 'pricesIncludeTax' is the pricing MODE: true means prices are entered tax-inclusive (VAT/consumption-tax markets — the tax is backed out of the price and Shop Settings shows this single rate instead of the per-method matrix), false means tax is added on top at settlement (Canada/US). Display names come from each language file's 'TaxJurisdiction.<code>' key — those values are FORMAT strings carrying the local name of the tax and its punctuation, with '{0}' filled in from 'standardRatePercent' here, so editing a rate in this file is enough and no language file goes stale; a jurisdiction with no single rate to quote (Canada, the US) simply omits the placeholder. 'defaultCurrency' is used only to infer a location for shops that predate this setting; it does not change what a shop prices in.
regionComment: Canada ships as ONE country entry, not one per province, because no province quotes a rate here any more and three identical rows only ask the shop a question that changes nothing. The REGION machinery is untouched and still shipped-data-only: a code is free-form, so re-adding 'CA-ON' (or 'US-CA', or 'JP-13') is one line here plus a matching 'TaxJurisdiction.<code>' key in each of the five language files — no code change. Shops already stored with a regional code keep working: 'TaxJurisdictions.For' falls back to the COUNTRY entry that code sits in, so a shop saved as 'CA-ON' resolves to Canada rather than to whatever the home market happens to be, and it resolves back to Ontario by itself the day an Ontario row is added again. Keep the region keys in the language files for that reason.
taxNameComment: 'taxNameLabel' names the TAX ITSELF, as the suffix of a 'TaxName.<name>' key in the language files — what a receipt calls it when it says the price already contains it ('Includes VAT (6%)'). Declared only where prices INCLUDE tax, because that is the only place it is read: a tax-exclusive market adds the tax as a separate line and 'Order.Fields.TaxAmount' already names it there. A jurisdiction that quotes inclusive prices without declaring a name falls back to the generic 'TaxName.Generic'. It is a DIFFERENT question from 'taxNumberLabel': Japan issues a qualified-invoice number for a consumption tax, so the number and the tax do not share a name.
taxNumberComment: 'taxNumberLabel' names the tax number this jurisdiction issues to a business, as the suffix of a 'TaxNumber.<name>' key in the language files — Canada issues GstHst, France and Spain share Vat. Grouping is by tax REGIME rather than by location, which is what makes re-adding provinces cheap: every Canadian region would carry the same GstHst label. OMIT it where the jurisdiction issues no such number: the field is then not asked for at all, which is why the United States has none (no federal consumption tax to register for). Quoting no standard rate is not the test either: Canada quotes none and still issues a GST/HST number. Do not infer this from 'pricesIncludeTax' — Canada's GST/HST is a consumption tax quoted tax-EXCLUSIVE, so the two questions have different answers.
